- Interpretation: as documented, on both SDKs, and this is the control B-5 needs. A Task whose only stream the client cancels keeps running at both receivers: the receiver sees the client go — `client-gone` at the pre-dispatch ingress ledger, `consumer-gone` at the execution ledger, within milliseconds of the cancel — and the execution continues to `TASK_STATE_COMPLETED` with exactly one model call, which is what the preparation read from both SDKs' source (§8 item 1) and had no run behind it. One `SubscribeToTask`, sent by a separate process after the stream was cancelled and while the Task ran, attaches to that same execution: no second execute, no second Task, no second invocation, and the first event is the Task as it stands, working, with the id asked for, which is what the specification requires of a resubscription. So a task that fails in B-5's proxy-removal rows cannot be attributed to the loss of the stream itself: at this pairing, losing the only stream costs the Task nothing. The cancel is the client's alone, and the row shows it reaching the receiver at once: the two ledgers end 0.7–4.6 ms after the client's own stamp. The Go receiver was reached through the ingress from an in-cluster client for the first time in this lab — the lab's earlier worker-through-ingress rows are the out-of-cluster curl of the A.3 matrix and the replay harness, both of which set that header themselves — by the Host setting the author's note of 2026-09-22 adds, and the reading that made the note necessary is in the run directory. The one asymmetry between the halves is recorded rather than smoothed: the Go card GET crosses the ingress with that Host, while the Python card GET crosses `agw-central`'s `lab/orchestrator` route, because the Python receiver's card advertises the ingress and its Service address is what the client resolves from. Not covered here: no proxy was removed, restarted or replaced — that is B-5a and B-5b, and the `agw-central` variant with it; a stream cut by anything but the client itself, which is what a removed proxy will do; any k other than 5 s and any N other than 45 s; a resubscription sent more than once, or sent while the stream was still open; and the wall-clock intervals of the two sleep-affected repetitions named above.
- Follow-up: none.

## Experiment B / both proxies / B-5a, the removal measured — when does each way of removing a proxy end an open stream, and when does the successor serve?

- Versions: k8s=v1.37.0@sha256:a1ed56cfb0e7b93589bdf97c8cd566405a265939e3620fc4f5de89adff580ae5 istio=1.31.0 agentgateway=v1.5.0 gateway-api=v1.6.2, experimental a2a-spec=3303592588e388e62e0f69f701af531d2f4e3991 a2a-go=v2.5.0 a2a-python=1.1.4 openai-python=3.16.2 (six of the eight read back from the cluster, `versions-readback.txt`, by the committed `versions-readback.sh` of 2026-09-20 unedited; `a2a-go` and `a2a-spec` are not on the cluster and that script reads them at the built tree, from `go.mod` and from `versions.yaml`)
- Environment: kind
- Method: the author's note of 2026-09-20 (`docs/proposal-notes.md`, "Experiment B on the agentgateway-only topology"), D5 — "what each method does to an open stream is measured first — a graceful delete, a forced delete and a rollout — and the experiment then uses the forced delete". **This step measures the stimulus and nothing else.** **No rebuild**, because no deployed path changed: every deployed path at this branch's HEAD is byte-equal to the tree the standing cluster was built from, the commit `feat(loadgen,deploy,experiments): CLIENT_HOST, every request names the host it is given, and the knobs Job template renders it empty on every existing row` (deployed subtrees `deploy` f89a4719, `agents` 324396fd, `fixtures` d143d670, `internal` f63b96cc, `experiments/lib` bad5771f, `Makefile` 7244d671, `.ko.yaml` 2dcd1989, `kind-config.yaml` aa98aa46, `go.mod` a8314e0b, `go.sum` 53b265e5, and all eleven `experiments/*.sh` blobs; read 19:17:43Z). This step's driver and counter live under `experiments/runs/`, which the rebuild rule does not name, so this record carries no rebuild and no standard proof. **The grid**: 2 proxies (`agentgateway-ingress`, `agw-central`) × 3 methods (graceful delete, forced delete `--grace-period=0 --force`, `rollout restart`) × 5 repetitions, one at a time, 30 in all, each its own work item, driven by `rows.sh` one variant per invocation and counted by `counts.py`, both in the run directory. **One receiver, the Go receiver, and the entry says what that costs.** The brief's grid names no receiver and the streaming client is the load client (`a2a-go`) in every B row by the author's note of 2026-09-20, so the client SDK does not vary either; the Go receiver was chosen because on B-4's measured paths it puts each proxy on exactly one leg of a repetition — the ingress carries the A2A stream (B-4: 80 of 80 arrivals from the ingress pod, 0 from `agw-central`) and `agw-central` carries only the model call — which is what makes each removal attributable, where the Python receiver's card GET would put both proxies inside one repetition. The cost is that the `agw-central` variants measure the drain on the in-flight **model** call over the HBONE-terminating listener and not on the A2A stream; that is precisely the leg §6.2's second hypothesis is about, so it is the reading that discriminates rather than a gap. B-5b runs both receivers. **The path** is B-4's: the ingress's Service with `CLIENT_DIAL=target` and `CLIENT_HOST=worker.lab.internal`, by the author's second note of 2026-09-22. **Per repetition**: the mock reset and armed `{mode: delay, lwi, delay_ms: 45000}`; `kubectl logs -f` started on the pod about to be removed **before anything is sent**, so its access lines and its drain lines survive the pod; ONE `SendStreamingMessage` with `CANCEL_AFTER_MS` empty and `TASK_ID` empty — nothing cancels, the proxy is what ends the stream; when the client's own lines show the `status-update` at `TASK_STATE_WORKING`, so the stream is open and carrying events, the driver waits 2 000 ms and removes the proxy once, stamping the command on the host clock; the successor is watched through the Kubernetes API alone; ONE probe request of the row's own kind — a second Job, `MODE=stream`, nothing armed, its own logical work item `<work item>-p` and its own ledgers — is applied the moment the successor is first seen Ready, one send, no retry, never repeated; then the collection waits for the two lines that land last and takes the three ledgers, both pods' logs and the other proxy's access lines. **N = 45 000 ms**, unchanged from B-3 and B-4: it is the only N this lab has measured the path to carry with no timeout set anywhere, and it keeps this stimulus comparable with the B-4 control. Its consequence is stated rather than discovered: the removal is 2 s after WORKING, so the stream has about 43 s of life left, and 43 s is under 60 s — a cut that fell at the pod's 60 s grace could not be seen at the client at any N under the callers' 60 s ceilings, and no ceiling was moved. In such a repetition the recorded outcome would be "not observable at this N" and the discriminators would be the removed pod's own drain lines and how long it actually lived. **No repetition needed that**: every one of the 30 streams ended inside the window. **Clocks.** Every interval column names the pair it joins — `_h2h` both the driver's own host stamps, `_h2c` a host stamp against a cluster or API-server stamp, `_c2c` both inside the cluster, `_s1` an API-server stamp's second resolution — and the removal is anchored on four: the command (host), the pod's `deletionTimestamp` (API server), the removed pod's own log (proxy pod) and the client, ledger and mock stamps (cluster). Before the counted variants, **two dry repetitions** were sent and are kept whole under `dry/`, named here as sent and not counted.
- Result: run outputs under `experiments/runs/2026-09-22-b5a-removal/`; `removal/summary.csv` is one line per repetition and `counts.txt` the tallies. **No host power event fell in this task's window at all** (`sleep-events.csv`, written by B-4's `sleep-events.sh` byte-identical, bounded to 19:18:32Z–19:54:22Z, holds its header and no event), so all 30 repetitions are clean and every `_h2c` figure is readable. All six drivers exited 0 and every between-variant proof passed before and after each variant. **Seconds from the removal command to the client's stream end** (`rm_to_client_stream_end_ms_h2c`, host command to client pod clock), and what the client read: **ingress graceful 20 042.8–20 053.2 ms**; **ingress forced 35.6–43.3 ms**; **ingress rollout 21 643.7–27 268.5 ms** — all fifteen `stream_end: error` with the SDK text `SSE stream error: unexpected EOF`, 2 events (task/SUBMITTED then status-update/WORKING), `terminal_seen` false, `http_status` 200 `text/event-stream`, `posts` 1, Job Failed exit 3, one pod. **`agw-central` graceful 10 046.5–10 065.5 ms**; **forced 2 055.1–2 078.8 ms**; **rollout 11 467.2–12 309.2 ms** — all fifteen `stream_end: eof` with no error at all, 3 events ending `status-update`/`TASK_STATE_FAILED`, `terminal_seen` **true**, Job **Complete exit 0**: on that proxy the stream never broke, it carried the failure. **The same moment at the two ledgers**: the ingress ledger's response line and the execution ledger's result line lie between 3.1 ms before and 0.6 ms after the client's own end stamp in all 30 (`client_end_to_ingress_end_ms_c2c`, `client_end_to_exec_end_ms_c2c`, both cluster-to-cluster); at the ingress they read `stream_end: client-gone` / `consumer-gone` 15 of 15, at `agw-central` `complete` / `complete` 15 of 15. **The proxy's own drain lines, and §6.2's two hypotheses, answered separately per proxy.** From SIGTERM on the removed pod's own clock: the drain begins 0.291–0.587 ms later in 25 of the 32 removals, 5 000.0 ms later in 2 of them (the span processor, below), and never in the other 5 — the five ingress forced removals, whose logs end at the SIGTERM line and carry no `drain started` at all; `minimum drain completed` follows 10 001.0–10 006.2 ms after the drain's start, 20 of 20 counted repetitions that reached it. Then the two proxies part. **`agw-central` supports hypothesis 2 and names it**: the last line comes 0.4–1.7 ms after the minimum drain, 10 001.8–10 006.8 ms after SIGTERM, and the WARN line **`hbone error: drain timeout`** is present in **10 of 10** repetitions that reached the minimum drain — the exact discriminator §6.2 gave. **The agentgateway ingress supports neither**: 10 000.7–10 003.1 ms more after the minimum drain, and 20 003.0–20 008.4 ms from SIGTERM over its ten drained counted repetitions with ONE at 25 002.7 ms (ingress rollout repetition 3, the span processor's, below) — two rollout repetitions sit above the graceful maximum at 20 007.3 and 20 008.4 ms for reasons this step did not isolate — no drain-timeout line, the bind reporting `bind complete Ok(Ok(()))`, and the pod's object leaving the API about 39 s **before** its 60 s grace would have expired (`deletion_to_old_pod_gone_ms_h2c_s1` −39 207.6 to −38 455.4 ms). **Both halves are on record**, verbatim from the pod log in `drain-evidence.txt`: what the proxy **announced** — `drain started, waiting 10s-55s for any connections to complete`, and again `minimum drain completed, waiting, not accepting new connections and waiting 55s for any connections to complete`, 20 of 20 — and what it **did**, which is to end the open request 10.0 s later on the ingress and 0.4–1.7 ms later on `agw-central`, never at 55 s. Neither Gateway sets `shutdown`, so the deployer's defaults are in force and were read back from the running pods themselves: `terminationMinDeadline: 10s`, `terminationMaxDeadline: 55s`, `TERMINATION_GRACE_PERIOD_SECONDS=60`, `CONNECTION_MIN_TERMINATION_DEADLINE=10s`, `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60`. **In 2 of 32 removals**, of which exactly **one is among the 30 counted** (ingress rollout repetition 3; the other is dry 1), the span processor's own shutdown stands between SIGTERM and the drain — `error opentelemetry_sdk name="BatchSpanProcessor.Shutdown.Timeout"` — and the drain then begins 5 001.0 ms / 4 999.99 ms after SIGTERM instead of 0.291–0.587 ms; that is this lab's tracing configuration (100 % sampling, collector in another namespace) and not the proxy's. The collector's own record for both of those pods is committed as `collector-reading.txt` with its command and read stamp: each was still reaching the collector before its SIGTERM (1.400 s and 3.477 s before it) and neither reached it again afterwards, so the five seconds are the span processor's shutdown timing out rather than an unreachable collector — a reading about those two pods and not about the other 30. **Seconds until the successor serves**: its Ready condition was observed 1 449.9–2 510.9 ms after the removal command across all six variants, and the one probe of the row's own kind was answered by the new pod at 1 818.3–3 254.2 ms (`rm_to_new_pod_first_served_ms_h2c`, the successor's own access line). The probe was **never refused and never retried**: 30 of 30 `stream_end: eof`, terminal seen, http 200, 1 arrival, 1 execute, 1 invocation `ok`, `TASK_STATE_COMPLETED`, and `probe_work_item_matches` yes in 30 of 30, so no probe line can be read as Job 1's. **What happened to the Task and the model call.** At the ingress, the removal cost the Task nothing: **`TASK_STATE_COMPLETED` 15 of 15**, exactly one invocation line, outcome `ok`, latency 45 000.4–45 004.6 ms, the terminal state reaching the ledger 42 894.8–42 916.6 ms after the removal — the stream was cut and the work finished. At `agw-central` the removal cost the Task everything, which is D1: **`TASK_STATE_FAILED` 15 of 15** carrying the executor's own text `model call: Post "http://model.lab.internal:8080/v1/chat/completions": EOF`, on **one** model attempt with retries off (`MODEL_RETRIES` unset, default 0; `MODEL_TIMEOUT_S` unset, default 60 s), and the mock's own line says which side went first — outcome **`client-gone`** 15 of 15, the 45 000 ms delay abandoned at 4 155.3–4 211.2 ms (forced), 12 130.1–12 190.5 ms (graceful) and 13 577.3–14 434.6 ms (rollout), each about the moment the proxy died. No `stale-closed` line appeared in any of the 30 and none is filtered. **The rollout against §6.4's derived `maxSurge` reading, with what each half does and does not establish.** What is established: at the moment the rollout command returned the old pod carried **no `deletionTimestamp` at all**, 5 of 5 per rollout variant, against one present in 5 of 5 for a graceful delete — so the old pod had not been asked to stop when the command returned. Its SIGTERM then came 1 463.8–2 376.2 ms after the command. What is **not** established by this design: the successor's Ready `lastTransitionTime` is at or before that SIGTERM in 10 of 10, but it is an API-server stamp at one-second resolution and the margin is 114.9–989.2 ms in every one of the ten (`successor_ready_lt_to_old_sigterm_margin_ms_c2c_s1`), so the true transition could fall on either side and the pair resolves the order in none of them — the counter says so in its own column, `ready_lt_margin_resolves_the_order`. The only fine-grained Ready reading here is the driver's own host-clock observation, which is a polling artefact and lands after SIGTERM in 10 of 10; and the successor's first served request is necessarily after it, the probe going out only once Ready is seen. Showing the order would need a finer Ready stamp than the API gives — the successor's own readiness-endpoint log line, or a watch recording the transition — and this step captured neither. A rollout is therefore a graceful drain whose SIGTERM is deferred by 1.5–2.4 s, so it ends the stream that much later than a graceful delete does, and 5 s later again in the one counted repetition where the span processor's shutdown ran first. **What an operator's record of the cut request looks like, per proxy and per method**: `agw-central` graceful and rollout, 10 of 10, an access line **is** written for the cut request and it carries **no `http.status` field at all** — there was never a response head — with `duration=` 12 130–14 434 ms as the lines read; `agw-central` forced, 5 of 5, no access line at all; ingress forced, 5 of 5, an access line reading **`http.status=200`** for a stream the client saw fail, landing 0.659, 1.430, 1.527, 2.684 and 3.858 ms before its pod's SIGTERM; ingress graceful 0 of 5 and ingress rollout 2 of 5. In the two ingress repetitions where it appeared, that line and a `connection forcefully terminated` line follow `binds drained` by 186 µs, so the absence in the other eight is consistent with the `kubectl logs -f` capture ending at the container's death and **not** with the line never being written — stated as a limit of this capture, not as a finding about the proxy. **Agent pods**: uid and restart count recorded before and after every repetition; `agent_pods_unchanged` yes and `agent_restarts` 0 in 30 of 30 — no removal restarted an agent. **The redirect check** (the B-4 review's carry, this step's reason for recording what each client saw): nothing was followed. `posts` is 1 in 30 of 30, every client read `http_status` 200 with `text/event-stream`, no client read a JSON-RPC error object on the wire, and across every proxy access line collected there are **0 non-2xx and 0 3xx** statuses; the one status-less line is the cut model call's, which has no response head rather than a 3xx. **No redirect policy is pinned at this tree** — `internal/httpclient.New` leaves `CheckRedirect` at Go's default and no test pins that a 3xx is not followed — and no code was changed for it here. **The two dry repetitions**, recorded and not counted: `b5a-ingress-graceful-d1-01` (19:26:39Z–19:27:33Z) and `b5a-central-forced-d2-01` (19:30:31Z–19:30:57Z). The first found a gap in this step's own method and is kept exactly as it stands: `make ledgers` ran 13 s **before** the mock's invocation line and the executor's terminal state line existed, because a stream can end long before the Task and the model call do — which is what B-4's control established — so that repetition has `invocations=0` and a final state of `TASK_STATE_WORKING`, and neither figure is a reading about the proxy. `rows.sh` gained `wait_settled` for it, which reads the worker's and the mock's pod logs, sends nothing, and waits for the terminal state line and then for the invocation line until the arm stamp plus N plus 30 s at the latest. The second dry proved the fix and is D1's case read cleanly. The 5 s span-processor delay named above appeared in the FIRST dry, whose removed pod was the one step 3 had created 2 h 22 min earlier; the other two are ingress rollout repetitions. **The cluster is put back**, and one thing is not: both proxies at one ready replica with their Gateway Programmed, 0 retry stanzas on every HTTPRoute, 0 AuthorizationPolicies, the mock reset with 2 resets after the last inject, neither receiver armed, the orchestrator untouched in its deployed mode (this step never switched it, having used the Go receiver only) — but each proxy Deployment is now at generation 6 with six ReplicaSets in its history, and the two `rollout restart` variants left `kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt` on both pod templates, which the agentgateway controller did not remove (`cluster-after.txt`). This task started no keep-awake and changed no power setting, and does not claim none was active: the agent harness holds its own.
- Interpretation: each way of removing a proxy ends an open stream at a different moment, and the two proxies of this topology do not behave alike, so B-5b's stimulus can now be chosen rather than assumed. A forced delete is the abrupt case the author's D5 names and it behaves as one: the stream is gone 36–43 ms after the command, and at the ingress the client's stream end, the proxy's own access line for that request and the proxy's SIGTERM all fall inside the same few milliseconds — the access line between 1.47 ms before and 2 µs after the client's end, SIGTERM between 0.81 ms before and 3.57 ms after it, in neither case in a consistent order across the five — so the connection dying and the process being signalled cannot be ordered from this capture, and the entry does not order them. A graceful delete and a rollout are not abrupt but they are not the pod's grace period either: on the HBONE-terminating listener the open call dies 10.0 s after SIGTERM with `hbone error: drain timeout`, which is §6.2's second hypothesis confirmed at the discriminator it named, and on the plain HTTP listener it dies at 20.0 s with no such line and with the bind reporting success, where §6.2's first hypothesis predicted about 60 s. In both cases the proxy announces "waiting 55s for any connections to complete" and does not wait 55 s with an open connection on it. **This is not a rule 11 candidate, and the first version of this entry said otherwise because its tracker search silently excluded pull requests.** Re-run both ways and recorded both ways (`tracker-search.txt`, fourteen queries each, every result including the empty ones, each recorded figure being the page the query returned under a limit of 20 and not a total, against the API's own `total_count` tabulated beside them): over issues alone nothing on point appeared, and with pull requests included the mechanism is already identified upstream in the project's own words and fixed on main by **#3334 "proxy: keep serving open connections during drain", merged 2026-09-14T23:10:53Z**. Two things about it were read from the API in this session and neither is what was first assumed: **#3337 "fix: honor graceful drain deadline" was closed WITHOUT merging** 14 minutes after #3334 merged, so it is a second proposal of the same fix and not a second merged fix; and **#3334 is in no published release at this read**, having merged 67 minutes after v1.6.0-alpha.1 was published, its merge commit seven commits ahead of that tag. **#503 "drain: do not start drain until min deadline has finished"** merged 2025-10-07, before the pin, and is what produces the 10 s minimum drain counted here. The lab pins v1.5.0 (2026-08-27), which predates the fix, so the measurement stands unchanged and every figure above is a reading at that release. What this lab adds is the counted behaviour at the pin — how long each removal method leaves a stream alive, on which clock, with which log lines, and what it costs the Task — not a report of a defect; a reader should read #3334 rather than file an issue, and **B-6 writes no draft for it**. The reproduction material is kept all the same, as the record of what v1.5.0 does: `drain-evidence.txt`, with the removed pod's log committed beside it. The second thing measured is which leg a removal is on, and it decides whether a lost connection becomes a lost task. Removing the ingress took the A2A stream and left the Task alone: completed 15 of 15 with one model call, exactly as B-4's control said a Task does when it loses its only stream. Removing `agw-central` took the model call and left the stream alone: the Task failed 15 of 15 on one attempt with retries off, and the client learned of it in the ordinary way, as a `TASK_STATE_FAILED` status-update on a stream that ended `eof` with a terminal event and a Job that exited 0. So the proposal's second clause — whether infrastructure recovery converts a lost connection into a lost task — already has one half of its answer at this pairing: on the proxy that carries the model leg it does, and recovery is not the deciding factor, because the successor was serving 1.8–3.3 s after every removal while the Task had already failed. Recovery is fast: readiness at 1.4–2.5 s and a served request of the row's own kind at 1.8–3.3 s, once, with no retry anywhere. Two further things are recorded because an operator would want them: at the moment a rollout command returns the old pod has not been asked to stop at all — no `deletionTimestamp`, 5 of 5 per rollout variant against 5 of 5 present for a graceful delete — which is the half of §6.4's derived 25 % `maxSurge` reading this design can show, the other half needing a Ready stamp finer than the API server's one-second one; and the record a removed proxy leaves of the request it cut is incomplete in three different ways depending on proxy and method — no line at all, a line with no status, or a line reading 200 for a stream the client saw fail. Not covered here: no resubscription, which is B-5b; no row of the experiment proper; the Python receiver, which B-5b adds; any N other than 45 s and any removal offset other than 2 s after WORKING; a graceful removal whose cut falls at the pod's 60 s grace, which cannot be reached under the callers' 60 s ceilings; and `agw-central`'s behaviour on an A2A stream, which this step's one-receiver choice deliberately does not put on that proxy.
- Follow-up: none, and none is owed. The drain behaviour measured here is agentgateway #3334, already identified and fixed upstream on main after the release this lab pins, with #3337 closed unmerged beside it and #503 already in the pinned build; `tracker-search.txt` records both searches and the API readings behind those three, and `drain-evidence.txt` keeps the reproduction material as the record of v1.5.0's behaviour. No `docs/upstream/` draft is written for it, by B-6's ownership of B's drafts and because one filed from it would duplicate merged work.

This task started no keep-awake and changed no power setting, and does not claim none was active: the agent harness holds its own.
- Interpretation: as documented, on both SDKs, and it is B-4's control with a removed proxy in place of the client's own cancel. Removing the proxy that carries the A2A stream ends that stream inside 65 ms and costs the Task nothing — the receiver sees the client go (`client-gone` at the pre-dispatch ingress ledger, `consumer-gone` at the execution ledger, within 2.5 ms of the client's own stamp) and the execution continues to `TASK_STATE_COMPLETED` with exactly one model call, 40 of 40, which is what B-4 counted when the client cut its own stream and what B-5a counted when nothing resubscribed. The one thing this row adds to both is the resubscription: sent once, by a separate process, through the proxy's successor, while about 40 s of Task remained, it attaches to the same execution in 40 of 40 — no second execute, no second Task, no second invocation — and its first event is the Task as it stands, working, with the id asked for, which is what the specification requires of a resubscription. So at this pairing the loss of the stream and the loss of the proxy carrying it are the same thing to the Task, which is to say nothing at all, and infrastructure recovery has nothing to convert: the successor was Ready inside 2.5 s and the one request sent to it was never refused. Two differences from B-4's control are worth naming because they are the whole difference between a client that leaves and a proxy that dies: the client's end reads `SSE stream error: unexpected EOF` here where B-4 read `SSE stream error: context canceled`, and the removed proxy's own record of what it cut is **misleading rather than missing** — 40 of 40 access lines read `http.status=200` for a stream the client saw fail, which is B-5a's reading reproduced eight times over and on both receivers. An operator reading that proxy's access log alone would count 40 successful streamed responses. Not covered here: the graceful delete and the `rollout restart` of the ingress, which B-5a measured with no resubscription after them and which this step did not use; `agw-central`, which is the companion entry; the Python client as a **reconnecting** client — `a2a-python` is exercised as a receiver only, by the author's note of 2026-09-20, and the streaming client is the load client (`a2a-go`) in every B row; any N other than 45 000 ms and any removal offset other than 2 000 ms after the client's `WORKING` event; more than one resubscription, and a resubscription sent before the successor was observed Ready; and the deletion and recreation of a Gateway, the third stimulus of the preparation's §6.4, which no B step has used.
- Follow-up: none, and none is owed. The one project behaviour this row met that is not the lab's own is the access-line timestamp, which this lab has already filed as agentgateway#3369 and which is already fixed upstream by #3370 in a release later than the pin; it is cited above and no new `docs/upstream/` draft is written for it, by B-6's ownership of B's drafts and because one filed from it would duplicate closed work.

## Experiment B / both receivers / B-5b, `agw-central` removed under an open stream — can ONE `SubscribeToTask` still reach a Task whose model leg the removal killed, and what does it get?

- Versions: k8s=v1.37.0@sha256:a1ed56cfb0e7b93589bdf97c8cd566405a265939e3620fc4f5de89adff580ae5 istio=1.31.0 agentgateway=v1.5.0 gateway-api=v1.6.2, experimental a2a-spec=3303592588e388e62e0f69f701af531d2f4e3991 a2a-go=v2.5.0 a2a-python=1.1.4 openai-python=3.16.2 (read back as the companion entry's are, `versions-readback.txt`)
- Environment: kind
- Method: the variant of §4.4 B that the author's note of 2026-09-20 adds — `agw-central` carries both the agent leg and the model leg, so removing it is the case the second clause of the proposal's sentence names, whether infrastructure recovery converts a lost connection into a lost task. **This row uses a GRACEFUL delete where the main rows use a forced one, on purpose, and B-5a is why.** B-5a measured the forced delete of `agw-central`: the Task is already `TASK_STATE_FAILED` at 2 055–2 079 ms while the successor is only Ready at 2 115–2 511 ms, so a resubscription could never reach a running Task at all and the row would have measured nothing about reattachment. The graceful delete leaves about 7 s — B-5a: the Task fails at 10 046–10 066 ms and the successor serves at 2 16x–3 05x ms — and that window is what this row uses. The companion entry's main rows keep the forced delete of `agentgateway-ingress`, the abrupt case the author's D5 names, and the two rows are therefore **not** the same stimulus and their cells are not comparable one to one; each entry states its own. `rows.sh` refuses any other pairing of proxy and method before anything is sent. **No rebuild**, the deployed subtrees and the starting state being those the companion entry lists and reads back (`cluster-before.txt`). **The row**, per receiver, 20 repetitions, one at a time, is the companion entry's in every other respect: the mock armed `{mode: delay, lwi, delay_ms: 45000}`; `kubectl logs -f` started on the pod about to be removed before anything is sent; Job 1 one `SendStreamingMessage` with `CANCEL_AFTER_MS` and `TASK_ID` empty; the removal 2 000 ms after the client's own `WORKING` event, stamped on the host clock; the successor watched through the Kubernetes API alone; Job 2 a second Job and a second process sending ONE `SubscribeToTask` for Job 1's task id the moment the successor is first seen Ready, never repeated; the task id read off Job 1's own event line, which **here is the only way it can be read**, because Job 1's stream is still open at that moment and has written no end line. **N = 45 000 ms**, no caller ceiling moved. The paths, the orchestrator's model mode, the clock naming and the two dry repetitions are the companion entry's.
- Result: run outputs under `experiments/runs/2026-09-22-b5b-removal-resubscribe/`. **No host power event fell in this task's window at all**, so all 40 repetitions of this row are clean. Both drivers exited 0 and every between-variant proof passed before and after each variant. Wall time: the Python 20 in 7 min 27 s (21:20:23Z–21:27:50Z), the Go 20 in 7 min 16 s (21:45:56Z–21:53:12Z). **The stream was never cut here — it carried the failure.** Job 1, 40 of 40: 3 events, `task`/`SUBMITTED` then `status-update`/`WORKING` then `status-update`/**`TASK_STATE_FAILED`**, `terminal_seen` **true**, `stream_end: eof` with **no error at all**, http 200, `posts` 1, Job **Complete exit 0**, and both ledgers reading `stream_end: complete`. Its end came 10 053.4–10 067.6 ms (go) and 10 046.1–15 070.1 ms (py) after the removal command, the two Python repetitions above 15 s being the span-processor case below; over the 38 without it the range is **10 046.1–10 085.1 ms**. The ledgers lie between 4.1 ms before and 1.6 ms after the client's own end stamp. **The removal cost the Task everything**, which is B-5a's D1: 1 arrival, 1 execute, 1 task, **`TASK_STATE_FAILED` 40 of 40**, on **one** model attempt with retries off (`MODEL_RETRIES` and `MODEL_TIMEOUT_S` both unset on the worker, `MODEL_MAX_RETRIES=0` on the orchestrator), and **exactly one invocation line**, outcome **`client-gone`** 40 of 40, latency 12 159.9–12 199.0 ms (go) and 12 119.4–17 201.3 ms (py); no `stale-closed` line appeared in any of the 40 and none is filtered. **The two receivers word the failure differently on their own state line, and this is a second SDK asymmetry on a second event**, recorded the way B-4 recorded its first. On the terminal `state` line of the same lost-model-call event the Go worker carries `model call: Post "http://model.lab.internal:8080/v1/chat/completions": EOF` in **20 of 20** and the Python orchestrator carries **`Connection error.`** in **20 of 20**; **neither text varies within its row** — one distinct text in each, and the Go text names the method, the URL and the wire condition where the Python one names none of the three. B-4 already holds one such asymmetry, on the *cancelled-stream* event, where the Go execution result line carries `error: "queue read failed: context canceled"` and the Python line carries no `error` key at all; that one reproduces here too, on the companion row's cut stream, 20 of 20 each. The two are on different events and neither moves a count. **The one resubscription reached the running Task, 40 of 40.** It arrived **2 052.8–2 803.9 ms** (py) and **2 074.4–2 413.2 ms** (go) after the removal command, and **7 488.5–13 014.9 ms (py) and 7 649.9–7 980.0 ms (go) before the Task's terminal state**, so `task_running_at_sub_arrival` is yes in 40 of 40, and `job1_stream_at_job2_apply` is **`<still open>`** in 40 of 40 — Job 2 went out while Job 1's stream was still carrying events, which is what this row's window is. What it got, 40 of 40: +1 arrival (`SubscribeToTask`) joined on the task id, **0 new executes, 0 new tasks, 0 new invocations**, both ledgers `complete`, **first event a `task` at `TASK_STATE_WORKING` carrying Job 1's task id**, then `status-update`/`TASK_STATE_FAILED`, terminal seen, `stream_end: eof`, http 200, `posts` 1, Job 2 **Complete exit 0**. **The drain, and §6.2's second hypothesis at its own discriminator**: SIGTERM 39.1–68.8 ms after the command; the drain begins 0.3–0.8 ms later in the Go 20 and in 18 of the Python 20; `minimum drain completed` follows **10 000.7–10 011.3 ms** after the drain's start; the last line the pod writes is **`binds drained`** in 40 of 40, 0.3–2.6 ms after the minimum drain; and the WARN line **`hbone error: drain timeout`** is present in **40 of 40**. **In 2 of the 40** (`b5b-py-central-graceful-r1-01` and `-r1-13`) the span processor's own shutdown stands between SIGTERM and the drain — `error opentelemetry_sdk name="BatchSpanProcessor.Shutdown.Timeout"` verbatim — and the drain then begins 5 000.8 and 5 001.3 ms after SIGTERM instead of 0.3–0.8 ms, which pushes those two repetitions' whole timeline out by five seconds (their invocation latencies 17 201.3 and 17 165.9 ms, their stream ends 15 065.3 and 15 070.1 ms). That is this lab's tracing configuration — 100 % sampling, the collector in another namespace — and not the proxy; it is B-5a's 2 of 32 reading, reproduced at 2 of 40 and confined to the Python half. **What the removed proxy left as a record of the request it was carrying**: an access line **was** written for the cut model POST in **40 of 40**, and it carries **no `http.status` field at all** — there was never a response head — with `duration=` 12 161–12 200 ms (go) and 12 120–12 230 ms (py), plus 17 166 and 17 202 ms in the two span-processor repetitions. B-5a's 10 of 10 reading, reproduced at 40 of 40. **Which proxy pod answered each request, Job 1's and Job 2's separately** (`request-attribution.txt`): both POSTs — `SendStreamingMessage` and `SubscribeToTask` — arrived from the **agentgateway ingress** pod, which this row never touched, 40 of 40, because on both receivers the A2A stream and the resubscription's POST cross the ingress and not `agw-central`. The card GETs differ by receiver and the difference is the path: on the **Go** row both cross the ingress too, 20 of 20, so **nothing of either Job touched the removed proxy at all** and the only thing it carried was Job 1's model call; on the **Python** row Job 1's card GET was answered by the **removed** pod and **Job 2's by its successor**, 20 of 20 each — the one request of this lab that has to cross the proxy just removed, and it was answered. The accounting closes exactly: five access lines per repetition, 100 per variant. **How many of the 20 sent a subscription at all**: **20 of 20 in each row**, all 20 arrived, all 20 reattached, **0 refused on the wire and 0 arriving after the Task had ended**; nothing was retried or re-sent, and a repetition that had sent none would have been a counted outcome. B-5a's table is why that number could have been below 20 here and is not: under the *forced* delete of this proxy the Task is already failed before the successor is Ready. **What the successor carried differs by receiver, and the difference is the path**: on the **Go** path the successor carried **nothing at all** — 0 access lines in 20 of 20 — because neither Job crosses `agw-central` on that path and the model call died with the old pod; on the **Python** path it carried exactly one line, **Job 2's card GET on `lab/orchestrator`, status 200**, at 2 051.1–2 801.7 ms after the removal, the Python card GET being the one request of this lab that crosses `agw-central`. So the least certain thing in this row — a resubscription whose card GET has to cross the proxy that was just removed — was answered by the successor, 20 of 20, and was never refused and never retried. The successor was Ready 1 632.5–2 391.1 ms (py) and 1 665.9–2 006.3 ms (go) after the removal, and Job 2 was applied 1 749.1–2 505.3 ms and 1 777.5–2 120.5 ms after it. **Agent pods**: `agent_pods_unchanged` yes and `agent_restarts` 0 in **40 of 40**. **The redirect check**: `posts` 1 for both clients in 40 of 40, http 200, `wire_error_code` 0 in 80 of 80 client end lines, **0 3xx** across the 200 access lines this row collected, and the only non-2xx is the cut model call's status-less line, which has no response head rather than a 3xx. No redirect policy is pinned at this tree and no code was changed for it here. **The access-line timestamp defect** named in the companion entry (agentgateway#3369, fixed by #3370, not in the pinned v1.5.0) touched 24 of this row's 200 access lines and cost **no** figure here: the Python half's successor figure is readable in 20 of 20, and the Go half's is absent for the different and stated reason that the successor carried no line at all. **The cluster is put back** as the companion entry records it, and this step changed neither proxy Deployment's generation.
- Interpretation: the second clause of the proposal's sentence now has both halves of its answer at this pairing, and neither half is about recovery. Removing the proxy that carries the **model** leg costs the Task everything — `TASK_STATE_FAILED` 40 of 40 on one attempt with retries off — exactly as B-5a counted with nothing resubscribing, while removing the proxy that carries the **A2A stream** costs it nothing, which is the companion entry. The leg the removal is on decides it, and infrastructure recovery is not the deciding factor: the successor was Ready inside 2.4 s in every one of the 40 and the Task failed all the same, about eight seconds later. What this row adds to B-5a is that the resubscription **can** reach such a Task while it still runs, and does: sent once, the moment the successor was observed Ready, it arrived 2.1–2.8 s after the removal and 7.5–13.0 s before the Task ended, attached to the same execution with no second execute, no second Task and no second model call, and was told the Task's state as it stood and then its failure — over its own stream, cleanly, with a terminal event and a Job that exited 0. A client that resubscribes here learns the outcome; it does not change it. That reading exists only because the removal was graceful: under the forced delete B-5a measured, the Task is already failed before the successor is Ready, and the row would have recorded a resubscription arriving after a terminal state instead. The stream itself is the other surprise worth keeping: on this proxy it never broke in any of the 40: it carried `TASK_STATE_FAILED` as an ordinary status update and ended `eof`, so a client watching only its transport would have seen nothing wrong at all. And §6.2's second hypothesis is confirmed again at the discriminator it named, 40 of 40 — the open call on the HBONE-terminating listener dies 10.0 s after SIGTERM with `hbone error: drain timeout`, while the proxy's own message announces waiting 55 s for connections to complete. Not covered here: the forced delete and the `rollout restart` of `agw-central`, which B-5a measured with no resubscription after them and which this row did not use — and the forced delete in particular is a case this row deliberately does not measure, because there is no window in it; the agentgateway ingress, which is the companion entry; `agw-central` carrying an A2A stream, which no path of this lab puts on it; the Python client as a **reconnecting** client, `a2a-python` being exercised as a receiver only by the author's note of 2026-09-20; any N other than 45 000 ms, any removal offset other than 2 000 ms after `WORKING`, and any resubscription but the single one; and the deletion and recreation of a Gateway, the third stimulus of the preparation's §6.4.
- Follow-up: none, for the reason the companion entry gives.

## 2026-09-22 — correction beside the B-5a entry (three figures that rest on an agentgateway access-line timestamp)

The entry above, `## Experiment B / both proxies / B-5a, the removal measured`, is not edited; this note is the correction, and the
B-5b entries that follow already carry the wording it gives. It was written while running B-5b, which met the same defect on the same
cluster and measured where it falls.

**What the defect is.** agentgateway at v1.5.0, the release this lab pins, renders the sub-second part of a log timestamp with its
leading zeros removed, so `19:52:06.082790Z` is written `19:52:06.82790Z` and reads, as written, 745 ms later than it was. This lab
found it, filed it and has it on record: `docs/upstream/agentgateway-access-log-timestamp-leading-zeros.md`, issue
agentgateway#3369 (filed 2026-09-07, closed 2026-09-08), fixed by pull request #3370, with the first release containing the fix being
the v1.6.0-alpha.1 prerelease — so v1.5.0 carries it and no stable release yet fixes it. Nothing new is owed upstream and no draft is
written for this.

**Where it falls, measured.** Over every proxy log line B-5b collected on this cluster it reaches **only the access line's own
stamp**: 47 of 400 access lines (11.75 %, which is the 1/10 + 1/100 + … a uniform microsecond field gives) against **0 of 1 986**
other proxy lines — SIGTERM, `drain started`, `minimum drain completed` and `binds drained` are all correctly zero-padded. In B-5a's
own committed logs the same split holds, and both denominators are given because both are worth having: over its **whole committed
run directory**, **17 of 176 access lines** are affected against **0 of 814** other proxy lines; over the **thirty counted
repetitions alone**, which is what its published figures rest on, **15 of 167 access lines** against **0 of 766** other lines, the
difference being the two dry repetitions committed beside them. The intended value is unambiguous, which is what makes a
correction possible at all: trailing zeros are **not** dropped — 240 of B-5b's six-digit fractions end in a zero — so a fraction
shorter than six digits means leading zeros were removed and the value the proxy meant is the digits left-padded to six.

**The three figures that move.** B-5a's counter took the successor's first access line after sorting that pod's log by the parsed
stamp, so both the figure and, where a file holds two lines, which line is "first" can move. All thirty repetitions were re-checked
against B-5a's own files; **three move and twenty-seven are unaffected**:

- `b5a-central-rollout-r1-01`, published **3 254.2 ms** — the **upper bound of the entry's published range**, "the one probe … was
  answered by the new pod at 1 818.3–3 254.2 ms". Its one access line reads `19:52:06.82790Z` where the proxy meant
  `19:52:06.082790Z`; corrected, **2 509.1 ms**. **The entry's range becomes 1 818.3–3 082.3 ms**, its new maximum coming from
  `b5a-central-forced-r1-05`, whose stamp is intact. The lower bound is unchanged.
- `b5a-central-graceful-r1-05`, published **2 395.0 ms**; its stamp reads 202.1 ms late; corrected, **2 192.9 ms**. It sits inside the
  range either way.
- `b5a-ingress-graceful-r1-02`, published **2 717.0 ms**; corrected, **2 514.1 ms** — and here the **identity** moves as well as the
  number. That successor served a card GET and then a POST; the card GET's stamp reads `.410Z` where the proxy meant `.000410Z`, so
  under B-5a's sort it fell *after* the POST and the entry records the **POST** as the successor's first access line. The first
  request that successor actually served is the card GET. The B-5a review's statement that the ingress successor's first line is the
  probe's card GET holds for the other ingress repetitions and is what the corrected reading restores here.

**What does not move, re-derived rather than assumed.** B-5a's Interpretation says that at the ingress "the access line between
1.47 ms before and 2 µs after the client's end, SIGTERM between 0.81 ms before and 3.57 ms after it, in neither case in a consistent
order across the five". That sentence is about the **cut POST's** access line on the five ingress-forced repetitions, and **every one
of those five stamps is intact**: re-derived from B-5a's files the offsets are +1.2, −1 468.8, −466.0, −372.4 and −288.8 µs, giving
1.47 ms before to 1.2 µs after, and the SIGTERM offsets −809.8 to +3 569.2 µs, giving 0.81 ms before to 3.57 ms after. **The sentence
holds**, and with it the entry's refusal to order the connection's death against the process's signal. The three affected lines that
do sit in B-5a `oldpod.log` files — in `ingress-forced-r1-03`, `ingress-graceful-r1-05` and `ingress-rollout-r1-03` — are all **card
GETs**, which that sentence does not use. Its companion claim, that in the two ingress-rollout repetitions where the line appeared it
follows `binds drained` by 186 µs, also holds: both access lines are at +186 µs on intact stamps, though the `connection forcefully
terminated` line beside them is at +208 and +199 µs rather than at 186 µs, so that one figure is read onto two lines about 20 µs
apart. Every other published figure of the B-5a entry stands: its whole stream-end table, the COMPLETED and FAILED counts, the
invocation counts and outcomes, the ledger offsets, the drain decomposition and the `hbone error: drain timeout` count all come from
cluster ledger stamps or from non-access proxy lines, neither of which carries the defect.

**How far the exposure goes, scanned rather than guessed.** Twelve committed run records hold agentgateway access lines that carry
their own stamp, and several hold defective ones — B-3's 70 and B-4's 14 among them. Holding one is not the same as computing a
figure from one: B-3's counter captures route, method, status and duration and no timestamp at all, and B-4's captures the stamp into
its dict but never reads it, every use being route, host, method, path, status or duration, and a `duration=` is a value the proxy
computes rather than a difference between two stamps. Of the committed records, **only B-5a and B-5b compute a figure from an
access-line stamp**, and B-5b's counter refuses to compute one from a defective stamp at all. Nothing else in this repository is
exposed, and nothing else is corrected here.

The derivations behind every figure in this note are committed at
`experiments/runs/2026-09-22-b5b-removal-resubscribe/b5a-correction/` — `rederive.py` and `rederive.txt` for the affected lines, the
three moved figures and the re-derived Interpretation sentence, and `exposure-scan.py` and `exposure-scan.txt` for the scan. They
read B-5a's committed files and write nothing back to them. No run record of B-5a's was modified, no figure of it was recomputed in
place, and its `summary.csv` and `counts.txt` still reproduce byte-identically from its own committed counter.
